backups.overview: East Twin Needle (7,868 ft) is the eastern and slightly lower of the Twin Needles pinnacles in the Southern Pickets, 0.55 mi west of Mount Terror and just east of its taller sister summit, West Twin Needle (7,936 ft). Both needles were first climbed together on August 17, 1932 by William Degenhardt, James Martin, and Herb Strandberg. Composed of solid Skagit gneiss, the pair rises above Crescent Creek Basin near the Mustard Glacier and is almost always climbed as a linked outing from one camp given the shared, multi-day approach. Besides the moderate line described here, East Twin Needle also has a notably harder, more direct East Arête (rated II 5.10a, climbed during the 2003 Southern Picket Range enchainment) and a 2022-established North Buttress ("Thread of Gneiss," 2,000 ft, 5.9, 9 pitches) - be sure you're on the intended, moderate line.
backups.beta: The South Route climbs East Twin Needle from Crescent Creek Basin by the loose south-facing gullies to the Eye Col (about 7,400 ft), the notch between East and West Twin Needle. Small chockstones low in the gully are scrambled past; the larger ones higher up are fifth class and are usually pitched, and a short scree walk finishes at the col. From the col the route climbs the steep summit block directly above, with a short hand-crack crux near the top that can hold ice early in the season; the summit is small, with a sheer drop to the east. Descend by downclimbing and rappelling back to the Eye Col, then down the south gullies with several short rappels off natural anchors. This is a different climb from the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) put up during the 2003 Southern Pickets enchainment, which is reached along the crest from the east and is not gained from the Eye Col.
backups.turnaround: At least 2-3 hours of daylight remaining for descent; turn around by early afternoon given the complex descent and potential for afternoon weather deterioration in the Pickets.
backups.rappels: Multiple rappels on descent (two 60-meter ropes recommended)
backups.face: South gullies to the Eye Col, then the summit block above it
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; the Southern Picket cross-country zones cannot be reserved in advance).
backups.comms: The Picket Range is a remote wilderness area with no reliable cell phone coverage. Satellite messaging devices (garmin inReach, Zoleo, or smartphones with satellite features) are essential for emergency communication. Reception for satellite devices may be limited by steep terrain and narrow gullies.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.
obj_haz: Loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the Eye Col
Fifth-class chockstone steps in the upper gully to the col
Extremely remote setting with limited retreat options

waypoints.name: Terror Creek logjam crossing
waypoints.note: Climbers' path fades to bushwhack here; cross Terror Creek by fording, or on a big log just upstream when one is in place (last reliable water before the steep, cliffy push up toward the Barrier).

waypoints.name: The Barrier ridge crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, exposed scrambling (harder late-season without snow cover) gains this ridge that separates the Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek Basin.

waypoints.name: Chopping Block saddle camp (above Crescent Creek Basin)
waypoints.note: Established bivy sites on the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block, used as base camp for both Twin Needles; Crescent Creek Basin, the talus/scree basin below the south-facing summit gullies, lies about 200 ft below.

waypoints.name: Eye Col
waypoints.note: Class-5 chockstone squeeze gains the notch between the summit gullies shared with West Twin Needle; rope up for this section.

waypoints.name: East Twin Needle
waypoints.note: East Twin Needle sits atop 'Eye Col' immediately adjacent to West Twin Needle.

backups.detailed_rack: Recommended rack includes a single set of BD Camalots from .3 to #2 (gneiss climbing favors cams due to parallel crack systems), a selection of passive protection (wedges/nuts), approximately 10-15 quickdraws, slings, cordelette, and two full-length 60-meter dynamic ropes. Given the gneiss rock type and mixed terrain, emphasis should be placed on camming devices that can handle variable crack widths.
what_to_bring: navigation (map/compass/GPS - route-finding on the Barrier is nontrivial)
extra water capacity for camp above 5,400 ft
pro_tips: Climb with West Twin Needle from one camp
Camp at Crescent Camp (~6,050 ft) or the 6,400 ft shoulder above Crescent Creek Basin - both have nearby water early in the season
Carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT); this is one of the most remote objectives in the North Cascades and self-rescue/SAR response times are long
Confirm which line you're on - East Twin Needle also has a much harder East Arête (5.10a) and North Buttress (5.9) close by
watch_out: brush and route-finding on the Barrier
afternoon thunderstorms, common in the North Cascades interior in summer
limited or no water at camp above ~5,400 ft late in the season
backups.pro_needs: The South Route requires solid rock climbing skills at 5.7 grade with competence in multi-pitch trad climbing. Leaders should be experienced at route-finding on complex alpine faces and comfortable with modest class 4 scrambling. Ability to place protection quickly and accurately in shifting rock and gneiss terrain is essential. This is an alpine expedition-style climb requiring self-rescue competence and remote wilderness mountaineering experience.
backups.approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead drop about 200-250' off the ridge crest into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile cross-country (talus, slabs, occasional snow) staying near 5,800', to a camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050' near two streams fed by overhead slabs (reliable water, unlike the Barrier). From this basin camp, descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col and onto the route involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty (this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light) before reaching the col, from which the route climbs East Twin Needle's summit block directly above.
backups.descent_text: Most parties reverse the route: downclimb the south-facing gullies back to the Eye Col and continue down into Crescent Creek Basin, a mix of class 4 downclimbing and short rappels off natural anchors (rock horns and slings - no bolted stations reported) on loose rock; expect 1-3 short single-rope rappels depending on snow coverage and the exact gully taken. East Twin Needle is frequently climbed in combination with West Twin Needle as part of a Southern Pickets enchainment; in that case parties continue the ridge west and exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch rather than re-descending the Eye Col gullies. That exit is better documented: two rappels using double 60m ropes are needed below the notch to get past vertical slabs, landing on grass and sloping rock around 6,800'; from there the route continues down a south gully with additional short rappels over vertical rock above a lingering snowfield before regaining Crescent Creek Basin. All anchors encountered on this descent are natural (horns, chockstones, slings) - carry cord/webbing for anchor building and expect to leave gear. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: back up and over the Chopping Block ridge, down The Barrier (roughly 4,300' of descent to Terror Creek - loose and brushy, arguably harder in descent than ascent), across Terror Creek, and out the Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Reverse the approach over the Barrier back to Terror Creek and Goodell Creek. There is no quick bail once committed above the Eye Col - retreat means downclimbing/rappelling the same gully system you climbed.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry permit for Terror/Crescent Creek Basin camps, and the Barrier is normally only safely crossable July-September once seasonal snow bridges and the approach brush have opened up.

days.note: A grueling cross-country day: old roadbed and steep, brushy boot path from Goodell Creek Trailhead past Terror Creek, then a loose, exposed scramble across the Barrier into the Crescent Creek Basin drainage. Most parties camp on a flat bench or col around 6,000-6,400 ft, close under the Chopping Block/Twin Needles group.

schedule.label: Ford Terror Creek, start steep climber's path

schedule.label: Cross the Barrier

days.objective: Reach camp in/above Crescent Creek Basin

days.note: An alpine-start day from camp: cross Crescent Creek Basin's snow and talus to Eye Col, the notch between the two Twin Needles, then scramble/climb the South Route to East Twin Needle's summit. Most parties use the same col to tack on West Twin Needle's easier class 2-3 west slope before returning to camp.

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start to cross snow/talus in basin while firm.

schedule.label: Gain Eye Col
schedule.detail: Loose gully between the two Needles: small chockstones low down are scrambled, the bigger ones higher up are fifth class and usually pitched out, then a short scree walk to the col.

schedule.label: South Route to East Twin Needle summit

schedule.label: Back at camp

days.objective: Summit East Twin Needle, tag West Twin Needle if conditions allow

days.note: Built-in slack for weather or recovery. Strong parties instead use it to climb another objective from the same camp, commonly Himmelhorn or Mount Terror's West Ridge, at similar cost in time and effort to Day 2.
days.title: Spare day / bonus objective
days.objective: Weather buffer or add a second Southern Pickets peak

days.note: A long reversal of Day 1: break camp, re-cross the Barrier, and descend the steep boot path and roadbed back to the car. Most parties treat this as a full day given the terrain and fatigue.
days.title: Descend back to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-4 day trip out of Goodell Creek Trailhead: a long, brutal cross-country approach over the Barrier to a high camp in/above Crescent Creek Basin, a big summit day tagging East (and usually West) Twin Needle via Eye Col, an optional spare/bonus day, and a long descent back out — roughly 16-19 miles round trip and 7,000+ ft of cumulative gain.

access.fees: NPS wilderness permit: $6 non-refundable reservation fee plus $10 per person, per night recreation fee (youth 15 and under free); no day-use fee.
access.notes: The Southern Picket cross-country zones cannot be booked in advance; permits for them are walk-up only, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace cross-country travel and camping (no maintained trail or designated sites in this zone); camp on durable surfaces around Crescent Creek Basin; pack out all waste; no campfires in the alpine zone.
access.permit: Overnight wilderness permit required year-round for the Southern Picket Range cross-country zone; these zones are walk-up only, so obtain a first-come, first-served permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (self-issue station available outside the WIC when it's closed for winter).
access.closures: No fixed seasonal closure of the trailhead itself, but the route is realistically in condition (largely snow-free, Terror Creek fordable) only from roughly mid-July to early September; check current NPS/trip-report conditions before an early- or late-season attempt.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: NPS wilderness permit (North Cascades NP has no general entrance fee).

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, with a fee
overnight_permit.where: Walk-up only: pick it up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center on the day of or the day before your start. The Southern Picket cross-country zones are not among the few zones that can be booked in advance.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to Goodell Creek Trailhead
road.status: Open year-round from the west (Sedro-Woolley/Marblemount side)
road.driveNote: Goodell Creek Trailhead is at roughly milepost 119, just west of Newhalem, on the portion of SR-20 that stays open year-round. It lies west of the highway's seasonal winter closure gate (typically Ross Dam TH, MP 134, sometimes moved down to the Newhalem gate, MP 120, in severe winters), so the drive-in is not gated even when the high pass toward Washington Pass is closed.
road.seasonalGate: Not applicable to this trailhead - SR-20's winter closure affects the section east of Newhalem/Ross Dam, not the Goodell Creek access.

climate.fall: Shortening days and increasing storm frequency by October; early snow can close out the route.
climate.spring: Heavy residual snowpack on approach gullies and the Barrier crossing makes spring ascents of the technical line impractical.
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window (roughly mid-July to early September) and the only realistic climbing season for this route; even then, multi-day settled weather is not guaranteed.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective; deep snow and avalanche hazard on all approaches.

bySeason.summer: Best season for climbing, but afternoon thunderstorms are common in the North Cascades interior; water sources above ~5,400 ft (Crescent Creek Basin camps) can dry up by late August.

emergency.notes: The Southern Pickets are extremely remote with no cell coverage and no easy helicopter landing zones near the Needles; carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) and be prepared for self-rescue - NPS SAR response here can take a day or more. Call 911 or trigger SOS on a satellite device; Whatcom County Sheriff non-emergency line is (360) 676-6911.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, WA - (360) 854-7245, noca_wilderness@nps.gov
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley, WA - (360) 856-6021 (24/7 Level IV ED; serious trauma is stabilized here and transferred/airlifted, e.g. to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle).

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed even during the Jul-Sep window; most Southern Pickets traffic goes to the neighboring West Twin Needle, Mt. Terror, or full-traverse parties rather than a dedicated ascent of this needle
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Likely fewer than 5 parties per season — no visitation data is published for this route; it is among the most rarely visited summits in the North Cascades

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very strenuous multi-day off-trail approach with heavy elevation gain/loss and bushwhacking into the Crescent Creek basin; expect long (8-12+ hour) approach days before the climb even starts
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy multi-day alpine load: overnight camping gear, technical rock rack, and approach/snow travel gear for a several-day trip

partner_requirements.approachTime: One long, strenuous day each way via the Goodell Creek/Crescent Creek basin to reach a Southern Pickets base camp before the climb itself
requiredSkills: Confident 5.7 traditional/alpine rock leading on loose rock
Off-trail wilderness navigation and route-finding in glaciated alpine terrain
Multi-day backcountry self-sufficiency in a remote NPS cross-country zone
Experience managing sustained exposure and loose rock (both already flagged as route hazards)
Basic steep-snow travel for the approach, especially early in the season
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climbers only — requires prior multi-day North Cascades approach and off-trail route-finding experience; not suitable for beginner or intermediate parties

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September, with August offering the most consistently dry, stable conditions

July.reason: Season opens as snow recedes, but early July can still carry residual snow on the approach and route before the mid-July optimum begins

June.reason: Typically still snowbound; both the approach and route are likely to hold significant lingering snowpack

August.reason: Peak of the 'best season' window — driest rock and most stable alpine weather

September.reason: Early September can still work, but fall is cold and stormy, so weather windows shrink quickly through the month

weather.typical: Remote alpine climate with a midsummer optimum: snowbound in spring, best conditions in summer, cold and stormy by fall, severe and rarely attempted in winter
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes are common in North Cascades alpine terrain in summer, though no storm-frequency data specific to this route was found

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained exposure on alpine rock compounded by already-flagged loose rock; given the route's remoteness ('remoteness'), a fall or injury here means a very difficult multi-day evacuation with no easy rescue access

avalanche.zone: N/A - no NWAC forecast zone specifically represents the remote Southern Pickets; this is a dry-season alpine rock route rather than a winter/spring avalanche objective

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on the South Route itself; early-season parties may cross residual snowfields on the approach, but the route is not glaciated

gaps: The 'South Route' (III, 5.7) grade/line is not independently confirmed against a named guidebook topo; published sources instead document a much harder East Arête (II 5.10a, 2003 enchainment) and North Buttress (5.9, 2022) on this peak - verify beta before relying on 5.7 as the crux.
Approach mileage to the Barrier varies 3.5-4.5 mi by source; gain_ft given here is net trailhead-to-summit, not cumulative.
No confirmed pitch count or belay-by-belay detail exists for the South Route itself.
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Goodell Creek group-camp trailhead off SR-20 near Newhalem

backups.rope_note: Picket Range alpine rock route by the Eye Col; the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) is a separate line. Standard alpine rack, glacier approach gear (ice axe/crampons) for Crescent Creek basin approach, 60m rope for multi-pitch rock, plus a second 60m rope for the double-rope rappels if you descend by the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch.
backups.corrections: Top-level grade field previously read "Grade III, 5.7", self-contradicting this row own rock_grade (5.10a) and its own beta text, which quotes the FA account directly: "It is graded II 5.10a." No independently-documented, distinctly-named 5.7 "South Route" was found separate from this line. Fixed grade to "Grade II, 5.10a" to match the row own corroborated sub-fields. Resolved 2026-07-28.

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Eye Col
approach_variants.notes: From the basin camp below Mount Terror around 6,050 ft, head west and drop about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek. Traverse north through Crescent Creek Basin, keeping the party together through the scree to limit rockfall and hugging the cliffs, then make a rising traverse beneath the Eye Col gully that carries you past an adjacent buttress rather than straight up at it. The notch at about 7,400 ft is reached by continuing PAST a gully that would otherwise force a rappel — that decoy gully is the thing to walk by. The last stretch to the col is scree you walk up rather than rock you climb.
hazards: Constantly falling rock in the Eye Col gully
Steep, loose gully climbing with genuine route-finding uncertainty on this south side
Disorienting in cloud or low light — the south side carries comparatively sparse route information
A multi-day committing approach over The Barrier before any of this begins
approach_variants.baseFinding: CHOCKSTONES ARE THE GATE, AND THE VIEW THROUGH THE COL IS THE CONFIRMATION. Going up toward the Eye Col, the small chockstones low in the gully present no real problem and are scrambled past; higher, the LARGER chockstones put the ground into fifth class, and that size change is where the rope comes out. If you are still stepping over rubble you are low; if you are stemming past a jammed block you are at the transition. The Eye Col itself is the notch between East and West Twin Needle at about 7,400 ft, gained on scree from the south, and it announces itself: from it you get your first sight through the gap to the Northern Pickets, and East Twin Needle stands directly above it. Know which line you intend before you leave the col — the Eye Col sits on the WEST side of East Twin Needle, while the peak's hard, tremendously exposed east arete is on the opposite flank and is reached along the ridge from the east, not from here.

climbing_route.label: South-facing gullies to the Eye Col
climbing_route.notes: From the basin camp below Mount Terror (~6,050'), descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty — this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light.

climbing_route.label: Eye Col to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the Eye Col, climb the steep summit block of East Twin Needle directly above the notch; the crux is a short hand crack near the top, which can hold ice early in the season. Reverse it by downclimbing and rappelling to the col.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the south side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

backups.name: King Kong - Gorillas Direct Direct
backups.fa: Sol Wertkin & Jon Gleason, 2016 (freed by Sol Wertkin)
gear: Alpine trad rack: alien/TCU to #4 cams
hazards: Sections of dirty, loose rock have required active cleaning on the upper pitches
backups.overview: The hardest currently-documented free route on Mount Stuart: begins on the original four pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, cuts left on a ledge system, joins two pitches of Gorillas Direct, then finishes independently with a two-pitch direct headwall finish up a striking splitter crack ('Empire State Building', 5.12a).
backups.beta: Grade: IV 5.11+ alpine rock climb (5.12a on some topos). Route length: 900 feet (8 pitches) on West Face Wall. First free ascent: September 9, 2016, by Sol Wertkin with Jon Gleason. Route climbs first 4 pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, moves left onto Gorillas Direct (2 pitches), then climbs 2-pitch direct finish up aesthetic splitter crack on overhanging headwall (5.11d crux). Connector pitch (5.10b): roof bulge, stem-box, runout overhanging jug climbing. Headwall pitch (5.11d): slabby steps, vertical features, meaty hand/fist jams, wild layback sequences. Required gear: double rack cams/nuts (small-medium), two fixed nuts at headwall top. Best season: late summer through early September (before fall storms and snow). Hazards: significant runouts between protection placements, loose rock with hidden chock stones, 30+ meters of overhanging exposure on headwall, alpine weather exposure risk (unplanned bivy possible).
backups.rappels: Single-rope rappel from a fixed anchor off the descent bench, then downclimb to Stuart Pass
backups.face: West Face Wall (between Goat Pass and Stuart Pass)
backups.permit: The Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Creek approach is outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit applies. A free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the trailhead box is all that is needed, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Digital Day Pass to park ($5 per day, $30 annually).
backups.descent: Follow the West Ridge to the summit, or descend the main W Ridge gully via scrambling/downclimbing, breaking skier's right onto a large bench, single-rope rappel from a fixed anchor, then downclimb to Stuart Pass bivy sites.
obj_haz: remote, committing free climbing at the grade

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd)
waypoints.directions: The Esmeralda Basin / Lake Ingalls Trailhead is at the end of FS-9737 off the North Fork Teanaway Road, at about 4,270 ft, and the Ingalls Way Trail starts from the parking area. It is the same trailhead and the same walk in as the other routes on Stuart's West Face Wall, so you are sharing it with the Gorillas in the Mist and Gorillas Direct parties. The approach is long enough that most parties camp near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek rather than trying it from the car in a day.

waypoints.name: Mount Stuart summit area
waypoints.note: Direct-start/direct-finish variation of Gorillas Direct on the same West Face Wall; tops out near the true summit.

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning; many parties bivy at Stuart Pass

backups.detailed_rack: Standard alpine trad rack: single blue alien/purple TCU, doubles from green alien to #2, single #3, single #4, one set of nuts.
what_to_bring: Bivy gear for a Stuart Pass camp
pro_tips: Rope management matters on the Monkey Traverse (P3) and other horizontal sections
backups.watch_out:
High-grade 5.11d sustained climbing
Serious exposure throughout route
Weather sensitivity - afternoon storms dangerous at altitude
Complex route-finding on ascent and descent
Altitude hazard compounds climbing difficulty
backups.pro_needs: Sparse protection reported on some traversing sections (notably P6); solid gear on the crack pitches.
backups.best_season: July through September, dry rock conditions on a west-facing, afternoon-sun wall.
backups.approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3), then continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge, and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft). The West Face Wall, home to the Gorillas routes (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek.
backups.descent_text: Quickest descent follows the main gully of the West Ridge via scrambling and downclimbing before breaking skier's right onto a large bench with a single-rope rappel option, then downclimbing to bivy sites at Stuart Pass.
backups.bail: Shared ledge systems with Gorillas in the Mist/Gorillas Direct offer some low-wall retreat options; above the Monkey Traverse, retreat becomes committing.

pitch_detail.notes: Start from a small ledge just above the snow on the obvious hand-and-finger splitter. Mantle out the top, pass a tree onto a ledge, then climb a short corner into a chimney and belay above it. The tree has slings around it that are handy for hauling a pack.

Go left up hanging corners around several arêtes, shuffle a short wide section à cheval, then traverse left on slab along an exposed crack. Skip the bolted belay and keep going left on slab through a short face crux to a large slung pillar. Rope drag is severe, so many parties split this pitch.

The Monkey Traverse. Climb the corner of the pillar, then swing right along an exposed horizontal crack to a large sloping ledge. Protect the traverse well for the second and extend placements to manage the rope.

Climb up, then slightly left into a V-slot. Finger cracks and varied stemming weave left, right and left again to the big midway ledge. Here the original Gorillas in the Mist breaks right onto 5.8 ground; King Kong heads left.
Move the belay about 25 ft left to the base of a striking corner crack. A crux start leads into a clean-lined corner and a good belay ledge. This pitch and the next are shared with Gorillas Direct.

A short, stout corner crack ends in a mantle onto a ledge. Continue up the crack onto slab where protection is sparse, traverse right-to-left into another corner crack, and finish with a rightward traverse to a two-pin belay. Back the pins up with small nuts.

Fifth Avenue. Climb the corner and the roof bulge above, move right then left into a stem-box, then go right on steep jugs with spaced protection to a two-bolt anchor at the base of the headwall. Grades given for this pitch range from 5.10b to 5.10+; back up the anchor with small nuts.

The Empire State Building headwall splitter. Slabby cracks and blocks lead to vertical tombstone flakes, then a step left into a hand-and-finger crack and back right into the main splitter. It is sustained hands and fists with powerful laybacking, wide sections and chockstones, with a crux pulling the lip. Graded 5.11d by the first-ascent party and 5.12a on some topos. Two small fixed nuts remain.
A final fifth-class pitch scrambles to the top of the wall. From there most parties descend the West Ridge gullies to Stuart Pass rather than continuing to the summit.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: Road access is via the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, which is not maintained in winter. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is needed to park. This approach is outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit applies; the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit covers day and overnight use.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk. North-side approaches from the Stuart Lake trailhead are inside the Enchantment Permit Area and need that permit instead.

road.name: Teanaway River Road (FR-9737) to Longs Pass/Ingalls Creek approach, or Stuart Lake Trailhead (Icicle Creek Road) depending on route/face
road.status: Teanaway River Road: paved then gravel, generally passable to standard cars to the road-end parking (~4,243 ft) about 1 mile past DeRoux Campground. Stuart Lake TH access road (FS-7601 off Icicle Road) is steep/washboarded, high-clearance recommended.
road.driveNote: Roughly 2-2.5 hours from Seattle via I-90 to Cle Elum then Teanaway River Road (for Cascadian Couloir/south-side routes), or via US-2/Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth (for north-side/Stuart Lake approaches).

climate.fall: Climbable into early October in dry years
climate.typical: Dry, west-facing wall with afternoon sun

emergency.notes: No cell coverage on route; carry a satellite communicator.
emergency.rangerStation: Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee NF

Treat as a projecting/cleaning effort, not a redpoint attempt

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Dominant hazard is dirty/loose rock requiring active cleaning on the upper pitches (pitches 5-6)

approach_logistics.trailhead: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd)

sling_rack.cams: base rack as Gorillas Direct plus supplemental 0.5-#4 recommended for headwall security

backups.rope_note: Climbs first 4 pitches of Gorillas in the Mist, cuts into 2 pitches of Gorillas Direct, then 2 pitches of direct splitter headwall finish. Three pitches run ~55m, making 70m more comfortable than 60m.
backups.corrections: Route list grade given as 5.11d matches AAC/Supertopo sourcing.

Doubles from green alien to #2 cam

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the West Face Wall — same base as the other two lines on the wall
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the approach for the other West Face Wall routes. From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below the West Ridge and on to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camp at either pass.

This line is a direct start and direct finish grafted onto the existing routes: it climbs the first four pitches of the original line, steps left onto the middle pitches of the direct, and then breaks out onto its own two-pitch finish up an overhanging headwall splitter.

Because of that, none of the decisions on this climb are made at the bottom. The base is shared; what makes it this route is a pair of choices at the ledge system and again below the headwall.
approach_variants.season: Late summer into early September, before autumn storms; the headwall is the point of the route and it wants dry rock
hazards: Significant runouts between protection placements
Loose rock with hidden chockstones
Thirty-plus metres of overhanging exposure on the headwall pitch, with retreat from it awkward
Alpine weather on a west-facing wall late in the season
An unplanned bivy is a documented outcome on this route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SAME SPLITTER THE OTHER TWO ROUTES USE — a hand-and-finger crack starting on a small ledge 15 to 25 feet off the snow or talus, gained by a short scramble. There is no separate King Kong start to look for, and hunting for one is how parties waste an hour at first light.

SO THE REAL ARRIVAL TEST IS THE WALL, NOT THE ROUTE: you want the amphitheatre roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, with about 1,000 ft of rock rising straight out of the snow above you. Anywhere still on a pass, or anywhere the wall has petered out into talus, is wrong. And the aspect is WEST — this wall takes the afternoon sun, so if you are standing under a face that has been in shade all afternoon you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

WHERE THIS ROUTE ACTUALLY BECOMES ITSELF, which is what you have to know at the base because you cannot see it from there: four pitches up the original line, then LEFT onto the direct for two pitches, then the two-pitch finish. The connector out to the finish is a roof bulge and a stem-box on overhanging jugs; the headwall pitch above it is a splitter on a steeply overhanging wall with more than thirty metres of air under it and two fixed nuts at its top.

IF YOU REACH A LEDGE SYSTEM AND SIMPLY CONTINUE RIGHT, you are on the original line and will finish on it. Nothing will stop you or tell you. The decision is yours and it is made in the middle of the wall.

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

backups.name: North Ridge
gear: ice axe (if snow lingers near saddle/tarn)
hazards: loose rock on the ridge
long approach
unmaintained/fading trail past the old mine site
backups.overview: Abernathy Peak is the high point of Abernathy Ridge, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from Wolf Creek and Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing past an old mining camp at a small tarn and up a spur ridge onto the crest before scrambling to the summit.
backups.beta: Rather than the popular Scatter Lake approach, this line reaches Abernathy from Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing a spur ridge from a small tarn onto the main north ridge, then scrambling the crest — weaving around or over gendarmes — to the top. Route-finding is loose and 'pick-your-own-adventure' in spots; parties report it as noticeably harder and slower than the standard route.
backups.turnaround: Loose rock, exposed class 3-4 steps, and a long, largely trail-less descent mean parties should set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight for a slower-than-expected reverse scramble, especially in poor visibility or if unfamiliar with route-finding on open ridges.
backups.rappels: None — unroped scramble; no rappels reported by parties ascending or descending.
backups.permit: No wilderness permit is required to hike or camp in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No parking pass is needed at the Wolf Creek trailhead.
obj_haz: route-finding on an unmarked spur ridge

waypoints.name: Wolf Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of Wolf Creek Trail #527, at the end of a gravel Forest Service road west of Winthrop.

waypoints.name: Gardner Meadows
waypoints.note: End of the Wolf Creek Trail, about 10 miles in, and the usual camp. From the last campsites a faint path crosses Wolf Creek toward Abernathy Lake and the upper tarn. Not plotted on the map.

waypoints.name: North Ridge saddle
waypoints.note: Saddle on the north ridge crest roughly 0.6 mi north of the summit. The coordinate is an estimate, not a surveyed fix.

backups.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is carried on this route. Cross-referenced trip reports consistently describe the non-standard North Ridge (via the Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows trail and an old, largely-vanished mine boot path) as an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree to Gardner Meadows, then an unmaintained path/cairns to a tarn and a spur ridge onto the crest, then a 'pick-your-own-adventure' scramble along the ridge crest with 'a few class 3 moves' on a spur ridge. No party describes placing cams, nuts, or using a rope.
what_to_bring: helmet (loose rock/rockfall risk on talus and scree)
trekking poles for scree and talus
ice axe and/or microspikes if snow lingers near the tarn or on the spur ridge (common into early summer on this east-side, north-facing approach)
sturdy boots with good ankle support for off-trail talus
map/compass or GPS — the old mine boot path is faint to nonexistent above Gardner Meadows, marked only by occasional cairns and cut logs
extra water — long ridge approach (about 10 miles of trail to Gardner Meadows) with few reliable water sources higher up
pro_tips: The approach is long: about 10 miles of trail up Wolf Creek before the off-trail travel starts, so most parties camp at Gardner Meadows
Watch for loose blocks on the ridge
The boot path on the crest fades past the old mine site — expect route-finding on class 2/3 boulders and scree the rest of the way to the summit
backups.pro_needs: None placed — this is unprotected scrambling, not protected rock climbing. Hazard is loose rock/footing (talus, scree, old mining debris) rather than lack of gear placements; a helmet is the relevant safety item, not a rack.
backups.approach: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.
backups.descent_text: Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back toward the top of the spur ridge (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From there, most parties drop down the scree slope toward the tarn with the old mining camp rather than reversing the spur ridge; an old path leaves the crest and descends to the upper lake. From the tarn, retrace the rough off-trail line past Abernathy Lake back to Gardner Meadows and follow the Wolf Creek Trail out to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.
backups.bail: Retreat down the ridge to the approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Ridge-crest scramble from the top of the spur ridge to the summit, weaving around or over gendarmes; loose rock and unmarked route-finding.

itinerary.cal: The ridge and the slopes above the tarn can hold snow into early summer; most parties climb it July-October.

days.note: About 10 miles of up-and-down trail up the Wolf Creek valley, through forest burned in 2021, to the meadows at the end of the Wolf Creek Trail. The trail drops a couple of hundred feet right after the trailhead, which has to be regained at the very end of the trip.
days.title: Hike Wolf Creek to Gardner Meadows

schedule.label: Camp at Gardner Meadows
schedule.detail: Established sites near the end of the trail; more flat spots in the trees by the creek.

days.note: Cross Wolf Creek from the last campsites and follow a faint path that soon fades into old burn. Keep high above Abernathy Lake and traverse up into the upper basin with the small tarn and the remains of a mining camp. Climb the spur ridge from the tarn to the main north ridge (a few exposed class 3 moves), follow a short boot path past old mining debris on the crest, then scramble class 2-3 boulders and scree to the summit. Descend by the scree slope or the old path back to the tarn, return to camp and either hike out or spend a second night.
days.title: North ridge scramble, then out

schedule.label: Leave camp
schedule.detail: Cross Wolf Creek and head for the upper tarn, staying above Abernathy Lake.

schedule.label: Spur ridge to the north ridge
schedule.detail: A few exposed class 3 moves; then a short boot path past old mining debris.

schedule.label: Summit (8,321 ft)
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 boulders and scree along the crest.

schedule.label: Back to camp
schedule.detail: Scree slope or the old path down to the tarn; then retrace the line to Gardner Meadows.

days.objective: Summit via the tarn, the spur ridge and the north ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A remote trip, usually done with a night at Gardner Meadows: about 10 miles of trail each way, then an off-trail climb from the meadows to the summit and back.

access.fees: None at the Wolf Creek trailhead
access.rules: Wilderness regulations; pack out all waste.
access.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required for Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness via the Wolf Creek trailhead (a permit is only needed for overnight stays inside the North Cascades National Park Complex, which this approach does not enter)
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest / Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.passRequired: None at the Wolf Creek trailhead

road.name: Wolf Creek Road and Forest Service road to the Wolf Creek trailhead
road.driveNote: From Winthrop take Twin Lakes Road, then Wolf Creek Road, then a gravel Forest Service road to its end at the Wolf Creek trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Upper road snow closure in winter/spring

climate.typical: Drier continental NE Cascades climate; afternoon thunderstorms in summer.

bySeason.fall: Stable but short days; early storms possible.
bySeason.summer: Prime window; hot and dry east-side conditions.

emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital (Brewster, WA) or Mid-Valley Hospital (Omak, WA), both roughly 40 road miles away; Aero Methow Rescue Service (the Winthrop-based EMS provider for the Methow Valley) transports to these or arranges air transport (Airlift NW / Life Flight) for higher-acuity cases.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in Mid-July through September, especially when paired with the popular Scatter Lake day hike
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - Abernathy is a Bulger 100 peak (~98th of 100) so it draws dedicated peak-baggers, but the long approach (11+ mi RT via Scatter Lake, or about 10 mi one-way just to Gardner Meadows via Wolf Creek) and remote Twisp River access keep numbers small; realistically a couple dozen parties or fewer per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong - about 10 miles of trail each way to Gardner Meadows plus an off-trail climb of roughly 2,600 ft from the meadows to the summit; most parties camp at the meadows
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight pack to Gardner Meadows, then a light summit pack - no glacier gear, but bring layers for afternoon thunderstorms

partner_requirements.approachTime: Most of a day: about 10 miles of trail up Wolf Creek to camp at Gardner Meadows before the off-trail climb to the ridge
requiredSkills: off-trail route-finding once past Gardner Meadows
comfort with ridge-crest exposure and short exposed steps
judgment to bypass gendarmes (dropping right off the crest) rather than forcing the crest
basic wilderness navigation - upper route is unmaintained/unmarked
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable with sustained Class 2-3 scrambling on loose rock and exposed ridge terrain; should have prior off-trail scrambling experience before attempting this peak

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September - this is a dry-rock/talus scramble that needs the snow off both the approach trail and the ridge

July.reason: Prime window opens as the route dries out; early July can still hold isolated snow patches on the ridge, late July is typically clear

June.reason: Lingering snow on the ridge and approach trail is likely ('snow-covered; trails snowbound' in spring); road/trailhead access may also still be affected by late snowpack

August.reason: Peak dry-season conditions ('hot and dry east-side conditions'); best combination of trail/ridge dryness and long daylight

October.reason: Early season snow and shortening daylight increase risk; not part of the best-season window

September.reason: Stable weather continues but days shorten; early storms are possible later in the month

weather.typical: Drier continental NE Cascades climate typical of the Sawtooth/Methow area; hot, dry east-side summer conditions
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer - start before dawn (as already recommended) to be off the ridge before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate to locally high on the ridge crest - short Class 3 steps and gendarmes have real fall exposure, and parties report bypassing some towers by dropping off the crest rather than climbing directly over them; loose rock raises rockfall risk to any party members below on the ridge; the long, remote approach amplifies the consequence of an injury given self-rescue/evacuation would be lengthy

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer talus/rock scramble; NWAC does not maintain a forecast zone specifically covering the Twisp River/Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness area (nearest NWAC zone, East Slopes North/Washington Pass, is oriented toward the North Cascades Highway corridor, not confirmed to extend to this drainage)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; route is entirely talus, scree, and rock ridge scrambling

gaps: Exact round-trip mileage not independently verified (approach description sourced from trip reports giving mileage ranges, not GPS track)
Trailhead and summit coordinates are verified (USFS Gilbert Trailhead page; independent summit-coordinate cross-check).
GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/1NH08

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft, at the end of a gravel Forest Service road reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road and Wolf Creek Road), follow Wolf Creek Trail #527 to Gardner Meadows.

backups.rope_note: Unroped Class 2-3 scramble on faint paths, talus and a spur ridge to the crest, then along the ridge crest; steep snow or loose rock possible early season, carry an ice axe if snow persists, but no rope or rack needed for the ridge itself.

approach_variants.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
approach_variants.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE DRIED-UP TARN WITH CABIN REMNANTS IS THE PROOF, AND THE OLD MINE ON THE CREST CONFIRMS IT. Working west from the meadows, the tread becomes distinct only as you near a small dried-up tarn on the peak's northeast side, known to some as Nasty Pond. Beside it are the remnants of a small cabin and an old pot sitting on a fire pit. That wreckage is the marker — there is no sign, no cairn at the turn, and no maintained trail — and a good stream just below it is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising directly to the main north ridge; expect a few class 3 moves on it. Once on the crest you pick up a short stretch of boot path running through old mining evidence, with metal cables and other equipment lying on the rocks, and that hardware is the confirmation you are on the historic line rather than a game trail. The path disappears past the mine and the rest is pick-your-own-line class 2 and 3 through boulders and scree to the top. Coming down, the scree slope back to the pond is generally preferred over reversing the spur ridge.
